subject: zoology

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.31, SAQ 17). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. ADDED BEYOND THE BOOK: endemism (species found nowhere else) and the loss of a large part of the original vegetation are the two criteria by which hot spots are identified, and the term in-situ conservation for the four protected-area types; neither is printed in this book's answer. The book gives the count as 'about 34', which the card keeps.

steps.label: What a hot spot is
steps.why: Two conditions have to be met together — very rich and badly threatened — and a region that meets only one of them is not a hot spot.
common_mistakes: Writing only that a hot spot is rich in species. It must also be under threat.
Writing that a hot spot is a protected area. It is a region identified as needing protection.
steps.memory_tip: Two tests for a hot spot: very rich in species, and badly threatened.
steps.margin_note: The worker's name and the two-part definition. Three or four lines.
lines: The idea of the biodiversity hot spot was put
forward by Norman Myers.
A biodiversity hot spot is a biogeographic
region that holds a large reservoir of
biodiversity and is at the same time under
threat of destruction by human activity.

steps.label: Features
steps.why: Endemic species are the reason a hot spot cannot be replaced: if the region is lost, those species are lost from the earth and not merely from that place.
common_mistakes: Leaving out endemism. Species found nowhere else are what make the region irreplaceable.
Giving the wrong number. The count began at 25 and now stands at about 34.
steps.memory_tip: Endemic means found nowhere else, so a lost hot spot is a species lost from the earth.
steps.margin_note: Four short points, ending with the number. One mark.
lines: Features of a hot spot:
They are the biologically richest and the most
threatened terrestrial ecoregions of the
earth.
They hold a large number of endemic species,
that is, species found nowhere else.
They have already lost a large part of their
original vegetation.
About 34 biodiversity hot spots have been
named in the world.

steps.label: Examples
steps.why: The examples show what a hot spot looks like on a map — a large named region with a boundary, not a single forest.
common_mistakes: Naming a national park as a hot spot. A hot spot is a large biogeographic region, not one park.
Giving fewer than the three that cover India.
steps.memory_tip: Three for India: Western Ghats with Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and the Himalaya.
steps.margin_note: Three names as a numbered list. One mark.
lines: Three hot spots cover parts of India:
1) The Western Ghats and Sri Lanka
2) Indo-Burma
3) The Himalaya
These regions hold many plants and animals
that are found nowhere else.

steps.label: Legal protection
steps.why: All four are places where the species stays in its own habitat, which is why they are grouped together as in-situ conservation.
common_mistakes: Naming zoos and botanical gardens here. Those are ex-situ conservation, outside the natural habitat.
Giving fewer than four kinds of protected area.
steps.memory_tip: In-situ means in its own place: reserve, park, sanctuary, sacred grove.
steps.margin_note: A four-item list and the term in-situ conservation. One mark.
lines: Regions rich in biodiversity are given legal
protection as:
1) Biosphere reserves
2) National parks
3) Wildlife sanctuaries
4) Sacred groves
Protecting a species in its own habitat in
this way is called in-situ conservation.

insider_note: Four blocks, one mark each — Norman Myers and the two tests, the features, the three hot spots covering India, and the four kinds of protected area.
